He is infinite, inexhaustible, beginningless, unborn, not consisting of mind, free from conceptual construction, sinless, the Lord of all worlds, truly one alone, abiding within all bodies, abiding within all things,

Whatever collection of causal factors— whether Vedic (śrauta) or traditional (smārta)— exists in any given context, all that is to be understood as Brahman; indeed, the entire universe is Brahman alone.
Regarding "proliferation" (*prapañca*): according to the Śruti, "All this, indeed, is Brahman.

Or rather, it arises only for yogis born into a family of the wise; for such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to obtain in the world. (BhG 6.43) Regarding the words "having obtained" (*prāpya*) and "then" (*atha*): The word *prāpya* means having attained [this human birth]. The word *atha* signifies a transition to a subsequent state. It indicates that after having attained such a rare birth, one subsequently attains the state of yoga. Alternatively, *atha* may be understood as meaning "therefore," signifying that because such a birth is so difficult to find, one must strive with diligence once it has been obtained. Furthermore, it may be interpreted as indicating the sequence of events: first one attains this birth, and then, through practice, one attains the perfection of yoga. Thus, the text conveys that having secured this exceedingly rare opportunity, one should not waste it, but should instead apply oneself to the practice of yoga. This is the intended meaning.

"Whichever" means: O son of Kuntī, whatever state—whether a particular deity or another object—one remembers at the end when casting off the body, to that very state one goes, being constantly permeated by the contemplation of it and having an internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) thus infused. 6.
Since this is so—(Therefore, at all times remember Me and fight;
with mind and intellect dedicated to Me, you shall come to Me alone, without doubt. BhG 8.7).
"Therefore" means: therefore, at all times, practice remembrance of Me;
and perform battle, which is your own duty—this is the meaning.
[This applies to one whose] mind is surrendered to Me.
And you, whose intellect (*buddhi*) that is [directed toward Me], are one who has dedicated both mind (*manas*) and intellect to Me;
for the intellect is that which possesses the specific modifications of the mind.
In ultimate reality, the internal organ is indeed one;
however, the designation of its divisions is for the sake of establishing conventional usage.
"You shall come to me alone, without a doubt;
there is no uncertainty regarding this matter,
nor should this be doubted."
At the time of death, memory may even occur otherwise;
for Īśvara is omniscient and follows [the results of] karma.
The controller of the fluctuations of the mind. // 7 //
1. To demonstrate specifically the point just mentioned, he says: "They abandon... (p. 183).
"By means of a mind disciplined through the yoga of practice, with its function directed toward nothing else, one goes to the supreme, divine Person, O Pārtha, by constantly meditating upon Him.
Regarding the word "practice": practice (*abhyāsa*) is a continuous stream of identical cognitions.
This yoga of practice is the wedge that prevents the recurrence of heterogeneous mental impressions;
by means of a mind endowed with this and free from other activities, one goes to— that is, attains— the supreme, divine Person.
Reflecting upon that very thing with his mind. // 8 //
He further qualifies that very Supreme Person:
"One should meditate upon Him, the Seer, the Ancient, the Ruler, subtler than the subtle, the Sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable, who is effulgent like the sun, beyond darkness" (BhG 8.9).
"Kavi" means the omniscient one, the instructor, the controller; for thus says the Śruti:
"O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable, the sun and the moon are held apart."
"Abiding"—thus [it is said].
"Smaller than the small" means subtler even than the subtle;
here, subtlety is intended to mean the absence of any accumulation of parts.
He is even subtler than space;
because he is the ultimate cause of all karmic fruits, he is the sustainer.
The Creator is of inconceivable form;
it should not be thought that "this is that," for his form does not exist.
"Neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red..."— thus, because of the negation of form;
nevertheless, form [is attributed] for the sake of favoring those who practice meditation.

It is described as having the color of the sun, consisting of light, whose sole intrinsic nature is bliss, situated beyond darkness— that is, beyond the darkness of ignorance— and dispelling the cataract of nescience.
"He who should remember that which is self-luminous"—thus the meaning of the sentence in the *Uttaragītā* is concluded. // 9 //
1. the qualified (viśeṣya) 2. the qualification (viśeṣaṇa) p.

At what time, moreover, should one remember?— (Endowed with devotion and by the power of yoga, with an unshaken mind at the time of departure, having properly fixed the vital breath between the eyebrows, he attains that supreme, divine Person. (BhG 8.10)
"At the time of departure": at the moment of death, with a steady mind, with devotion,
with a heart gladdened by the remembrance of Him, and through the power of yoga,
by means of the stability produced by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) born of yoga.
The meaning is: having caused the vital breath (prāṇa) to enter the space between the eyebrows and having departed by means of the *suṣumṇā* channel. // 10 //
Having referred to the state that is to be attained, and intending to explain the means for its attainment, He says:

"That imperishable state which those who know the Vedas declare, which ascetics free from passion enter, and desiring which they practice the life of celibacy—that state I shall describe to you in brief. (BhG 8.11)
"That which" refers to this very syllable, O Gārgī— namely, the higher [knowledge] by which that syllable is attained—
they enter it, that is, they realize it.
Ascetics (*yatayaḥ*), being diligent and desiring that [goal], practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*), which is the abstention from sexual intercourse;
this applies even to a householder in all respects.

"Except for what is prohibited"—this means that for one who has not desisted from permitted sexual intercourse and engages in it necessarily during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*), there is indeed the state of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
That is the goal; that is the means for attaining that goal, [explained] in brief.
I shall speak in brief. // 11 //

"Having restrained all the gates [of the senses] and having confined the mind within the heart, placing the vital breath (prāṇa) of the self in the head, he remains established in the practice of yoga-concentration.
Regarding the word "all": having restrained all the doors of the sense organs, [he places] the mind in the abode of the lotus of the heart.
Having firmly restrained [the breath] within the Supreme Lord, by means of the Brahma-nāḍī emerging from the root of the palate,
with steadiness and excellent effort.
3. "Go forth"—this is the meaning.
Having caused the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to rise up from the self through the two [channels] named Suṣumṇā, and having placed it in the head, he remains established.
"Having taken up the yogic concentration (yogadhāraṇā)"—this is the meaning. // 12 //
"Uttering the single-syllable Brahman 'Om' and remembering Me, he who departs, casting off the body, goes to the supreme goal. (BhG 8.13).
"Om"—this is a qualification meaning the single-syllabled Śabdabrahman.
This is for the purpose of excluding [the recitation of] the *saṃhitā* and other forms of the Veda;
"uttering" means pronouncing "me," the Supreme Self.
He who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal— he who is all-pervading like space, omniscient, blissful, and immortal.
And as for what was stated in general— “at the time of death he comes to Me alone”— that is now specified.
Some here maintain that this refers to liberation by stages (*kramamukti*) and is not intended to demonstrate immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*).

They say: "O Satyakāma, this syllable Om is indeed the higher and the lower Brahman"—so says the Śruti. To claim that this [passage] describes the fruit of meditating with the support of the syllable Om is a misinterpretation.
Since this belongs to the section concerning supreme knowledge (*paravidyā*), and because of the formal proposition:
"That imperishable which those who know the Veda speak of"—how can it be described as consisting of liberation at a later time? (13)
And I am not difficult to attain for one who is constantly devoted—
(“For that yogi who is ever-disciplined and whose mind is focused on no other, who remembers me constantly and perpetually, I am easily attained, O Pārtha. BhG 8.14).
"Ananya" means one whose mind is not elsewhere; such a person is "ananyacetāḥ. "Satatam" means at all times, continuously;
"nityaśaḥ" means for as long as life lasts.
By this it is shown that while the goal is accomplished by the mere knowledge of the meaning of the sentence,
fully ripened knowledge capable of liberation arises through constant meditation.
"I am easily attained" means I am obtained with ease by one who is constantly disciplined; this is the conclusion. // 14 //
1. Uttering;
2. liberation in the form of a subsequent time;
3. of what else? elsewhere.
The means for attaining that state has been explained;
once it has been attained, what [remains]?
Regarding the phrase "a specific human goal":
"Having come to Me, there is no more rebirth, which is transient and a mass of suffering."
"Having attained Me, those great-souled ones who have reached supreme perfection do not undergo rebirth, which is the abode and locus of suffering.
(BhG 8.15) "Me" means: having attained Me, they do not undergo rebirth, the place that is the repository of suffering.
Upon reaching another state, there is a return;
he shows that the attainment of Me alone is the cause of non-return. // 15 //
"O Arjuna, all worlds, up to the world of Brahmā, are subject to return;
but having attained Me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth. Regarding the phrase "up to Brahmā": it means "up to the world of Brahmā."
The world or dwelling place of Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha is the Brahma-world (brahmaloka);
with the particle *ā* used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*), [the phrase refers to] those together with the Brahma-world.
Living beings are so called. But is it not said: "He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself"?

"His delay lasts only so long as he is not released; then he will be perfected"— since this scriptural authority establishes that for the knower, liberation occurs immediately after the fall of the body upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, how [can there be any other state] for those who know Brahman?
For those whose impurities have ceased, there is no returning;
likewise, there is abiding as long as the office [of cosmic governance] lasts.
Regarding those who possess authority— according to the *Śārīraka-sūtra*, those who are established in their office (*adhikāra*) for the purpose of acting to favor the world,
they [possess] authority over the realm of Prajāpati and so forth by virtue of the Lord’s command.
Their stay [in the body] lasts as long as their office;
and while they are practicing the remainder of their knowledge therein,
liberation occurs upon the exhaustion of those karmas whose fruits have already begun.
Whosoever among the gods awakened, each of them [was designated] by that name; because of their location, the inhabitants of that place were called by the name of that place itself.
2. "Whoever indeed" 3. "shall be liberated"—thus [it is said] 4. "the stability of those who possess the duties of office."
5. Because of the instruction of the Lord regarding the office of Prajāpati and others (p.
187), "that became [so]," this refers to the attainment of the very nature of Brahman.
"Indeed, evil does not reach the gods"— this [argument] is untenable, because it also implies a denial of rebirth.

To this it is replied: It has been stated that liberation occurs for all upon the exhaustion of the experience of the fruits of *prārabdha* (commenced) karma. And that commenced karma is, for some, to be experienced in a single body; for others, it is to be experienced in multiple bodies.

It is recorded in tradition that even an action performed in a single lifetime may be experienced across many bodies; for example, the ancient seer named Avāntaratamas attained the status of Vyāsa at the junction of the Dvāpara and Kali ages by the command of Viṣṇu.

Thus, regarding the lack of uniformity in the fruits of liberation, because it is attained according to various respective states— as stated in the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras]— there is no contradiction here, since the non-uniformity of liberation is observed by virtue of the gradations in the fruits of karma.
Having come unto Me, O Kaunteya, rebirth— that is, the taking on of a body— does not exist again.
For what reason is there a return for the other worlds?
Because they are limited by time.
For the Supreme, having attained the state of the cause, there is no falling away while abiding in the worlds of effects.
Because they are subject to destruction, their return is inevitable; this is what he says:
"Those people who know that the day of Brahmā extends for a thousand yugas, and that his night likewise ends after a thousand yugas—they alone are knowers of day and night. (BhG 8.17)
"Ten thousand": as it has been said— "The total number of divine yugas is known to be one day of Brahmā, and his night is of exactly the same duration."
A day of Brahmā, consisting of a period of one thousand yugas, is his state of waking;
this is a duration of time delimited by fourteen intermediate cycles (manvantaras).
A night of that same duration is the intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*),
which is the state of sleep for Brahmā.
Thus, day and night are calculated according to the reckoning of a year.
His lifespan was one hundred years; that was his state at that time,
because he had not yet attained liberation from that condition.
3. *avaśyabhāvinī* 4. *mahārātrim*: this is the reading in the *Manusmṛti*, p. 188.
[This is] of Brahmā. Then Brahmā is released;
the great dissolution occurs.
At that time, the elements beginning with earth also dissolve. // 17 //
In that regard, the activity of beings during the day and the night is described as follows:
"At the arrival of the day, all manifest entities emerge from the unmanifest;
at the arrival of the night, they dissolve back into that which is designated as the unmanifest. (BhG 8.18)

Regarding the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*): the unmanifest is said to be the indeterminate state; it refers to the subtle condition of the five elements as well as the individual souls (*jīva*) accompanied by karma and ignorance.
The Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is the presiding Lord; this very point is now explained. And so says the Śruti:
"Indeed, this was then unmanifest"— thus it is said.
And that which is manifest,
namely the moving and unmoving beings as well as the great elements, comes forth at the arrival of day.
But at the arrival of night they dissolve;

the distinction is that in that intermediate dissolution (avāntarapralaya) within the manifest world, there is the dissolution of all beings, both moving and non-moving, whereas in the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), even the primary elements (mahābhūta) dissolve. // 18 //
Avoiding the two faults— that performed actions would perish and that the fruit of unperformed actions would accrue— he says:
"This very same collection of beings, having come into existence again and again, dissolves."
"At the arrival of night, O Pārtha, [all beings] become powerless; at the arrival of day, they arise.
Regarding the word "beings" (*bhūta*): because saṃsāra is beginningless, there is for the karmas performed in previous kalpas a state called "stability" (*stimita*), which is not their destruction.
Based on that, moreover, this manifold creation—distinguished by the divisions of gods, humans, and animals—is [the manifestation] of that very same [consciousness].
Thus it is said: "This is indeed that."
Because they possess the same name and form, non-difference is designated;
thus, those names and those forms are produced.
Just as those very same rice grains are eaten even though the individual instances are different, so it is [in this case].
The rest has already been explained. // 19 //
1. Therein it was prophesied;
2. and [the existence of] individual manifestations;
3. and the destruction of performed karma as well as the arrival of the fruit of unperformed karma.
4. The state of those who are motionless, p.
that which has been clearly described—[therefore]...
"But beyond that unmanifested state, there is another eternal manifested being, which does not perish even when all beings perish.
Regarding the word *para*: it means "beyond," signifying the ultimate limit.
The Omniscient One is unmanifest because He is beyond the scope of the senses;
therefore, from that aforementioned unmanifest and insentient source, this sentient Supreme Self is eternal and constant (the Highest).
How so? That which does not perish when all things perish—this is to be understood as the Lord (Īśvara). // 20 //
"Unmanifest, He is called the Imperishable; Him they speak of as the supreme goal, attaining which they do not return—that is My supreme abode.
(BhG 8.21) Regarding the word "unmanifest": this very Unmanifest Supreme Self is called the "Imperishable" (akṣara) in the Veda.
"From that Imperishable, the universe arises here"— thus the Śrutis call it the supreme goal; having attained that abode, the place, they do not return.
This is my supreme [teaching]. // 21 //
Furthermore, by what means is He attained? To this he says:
"That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attained through undivided devotion—He within whom all beings dwell and by whom all this is pervaded" (BhG 8.22).
Regarding the word "puruṣa": with exclusive devotion, intent upon Him alone, one worships Him through praise, salutation, meditation, concentration, and so forth;
not any other deity.
Its definition is stated for the sake of ease of understanding:
"For he within whom all beings abide."
For the effect is contained within the cause, just as a jar is within the clay;
and by means of yoga, all this is stretched out and pervaded by it. // 22 //
The true nature of the Lord has been determined, and the means for attaining Him has been taught, beginning with the words: "At the time of departure, by means of the mind... and so forth.
And for those who have reached the Puruṣa, non-return is stated.
1. Valita.
2. drawn by that;
3. restrained.
Now, showing by way of distinction the path by which those who have gone do not return and that by which they do return, he says:
"But at what time the non-return and the return of yogis..."
"I shall declare that time, O bull of the Bharatas, by which those who have set out proceed. (BhG 8.23) Here, the mention of "time" (*kāla*) is intended to indicate the path (*mārga*).
[This refers to] the practitioners of *karmayoga*.
And for the yogin of knowledge, [the scripture] first shows the path of the gods and the path of the fathers, characterized by the rays of light and so forth, because of its preeminence. // 23 //
"Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice—departing there, people who know Brahman go to Brahman.
Regarding the word "fire": by "fire, light," the deity of the flame (arcis) is indicated.
Likewise, it is established in the Śārīraka that the deities of the bright fortnight and the deities of the northern solstice are the "conveying" (ātivāhinī) deities;
by means of them, those who have departed go to Brahman, the Supreme Self.
In that context, the primary meaning of the word "Brahman" is intended, and the world of effects is not grasped, because the subject matter concerns the Supreme Brahman.
Regarding this, as has been stated by some concerning those who travel by the path beginning with light (arcirādi-mārga):
The claim that there is attainment of the world of Hiraṇyagarbha is incorrect;
here, non-return is stated to be the independent state resulting from the attainment of Brahman.
And so it has been said: "The worlds, from the realm of Brahmā downwards... (24).

Now, as a relevant digression, the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna) for those who perform only ritual works— a path characterized by repeated return— is described; this is for the purpose of showing how those lacking true knowledge might be overcome by others.
1. The *ātivāhinī* [nāḍīs], 2. for those who go [to the higher realms], 3.
how indeed is knowledge supreme?
Smoke, night, likewise the dark fortnight, and the six months of the sun’s southern course— attaining the lunar light during that time, the yogin returns. (BhG 8.25)

Regarding the phrase "smoke": here too, "smoke," "night," and "the dark fortnight" indicate the deities themselves; it is not intended here that the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), night, or day are meant.
For those who perform the combined rite (samuccaya) and die at any time whatsoever, the path begins with light (arcir-ādi);
for others as well, it begins with smoke (dhūma-ādi).
As for Bhīṣma, his waiting for the northern course of the sun was [due to his specific vow].
In this context, the statement that "death is praiseworthy" is for the purpose of encouragement, not for the purpose of establishing a restrictive rule.
The remainder has its meaning already explained. // 25 //
"These two paths of the world are considered eternal, the bright and the dark;
by one a person goes to non-return, by the other he returns again.
Regarding "the bright": these two paths of the world are the bright and the dark.
In the eternal doctrine, because it is declared in the Veda: "By one [path] he goes to non-return; by the other he returns again. The restatement of the meaning is the conclusion (nigamana). // 26 //

To show that one who has direct knowledge of the two paths does not merely undertake action for its own sake, but strives solely for the sake of their integration because it leads to the supreme good, he says:
"O Pārtha, no yogin at all who knows these two paths is ever deluded."
Therefore, O Arjuna, be disciplined in yoga at all times.
(BhG 8.27) "Not these," [he said]. 27.
This very knowledge taught in this chapter is praised by means of the disparagement of other [paths], so that those who possess faith may become diligent in it. 1. Eternal.
2. It turns out otherwise: "Whatever fruit of merit is prescribed in the Vedas, in sacrifices, in austerities, and indeed in acts of giving... (p. 192).
"Having understood all this, the yogi transcends it all and attains the supreme, primordial state.

Regarding the phrase "in the Vedas": whatever fruit of merit exists in the four Vedas, in sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, in austerities such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, and in the gifts of cows, land, and gold—[all that he transcends].
All this it transcends.
How so? Having realized this knowledge, the yogin attains the supreme, primordial state—the state of the Supreme Lord, which is the first of all states. (28)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Commentary on the Gītā composed by Bhagavadbhāskara.
p. 193 Now begins the ninth chapter.
It has been stated that those who have gone by the path of the gods do not return—“Having come to Me, there is no rebirth.”
"It exists"— thus [it is said].
Now, wishing to explain once more the true nature (*satattva*) of that Brahman, which is endowed with specific powers and upon reaching which there is no return, he says:
Because it is utterly beyond the reach of the senses, even though it is explained again and again, it does not find a place of stability in the minds of some; therefore,
the Blessed One strives so that it may become firmly established in the minds of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
The Blessed One said:
"I shall declare to you, who are free from malice, this most secret knowledge together with realized wisdom, by knowing which you shall be liberated from evil. (BhG 9.1)
"But this" means: "But this [which I shall tell] is most secret for you.
The word "but" (tu) is used in the sense of emphasis.
Envy (asūyā) is the act of exposing the faults of others regarding their virtues.
To one who is devoid of that,
I shall proclaim knowledge together with consciousness.
That knowledge, knowing which you shall be liberated from the impurity of the bondage of saṃsāra—
gradual liberation by way of the path beginning with the *arcis* has been declared for only certain performers of meritorious deeds.
Now they say that immediate liberation is being described; that is incorrect,
for [liberation occurs] only by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*).
Having transcended the sphere of saṃsāra through the separation from the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), liberation occurs; one is not liberated in this very body.
Therefore, the claim that "liberation occurs right here" is a false tenet. // 1 //
That knowledge is praised in order to generate faith:
"This is the royal science, the royal secret, this supreme purifier; it is directly perceivable, consistent with dharma, very easy to perform, and imperishable. (BhG 9.2)
1. That which is 2. constructed by means of temples and so forth, 3. for some [people] alone... this portion, namely that "it is not a false tenet" (apasiddhānta), is most secret.
Immediately following this, on page 194 of the root text (mūlakoṣa),
it says "rājñām" (of kings), referring to kings such as Aśvapati, Janaka, and others.
And for them, this is a secret, pure, purifying [teaching] whose comprehension is direct and clear— that is, "pratyakṣāvagama";
the meaning is that this is not something beyond the senses (parokṣa).
Just as with the knowledge of Mount Meru;
"conformable to the Dharma" (dharmya) means that which does not deviate from the Dharma, being very easy to perform and easy to accomplish.
It is imperishable because it is the cause of inexhaustible fruit. // 2 //
"But those persons who lack faith in this Dharma, O scorcher of the foe, failing to reach Me, return to the path of the cycle of death. (BhG 9.3)
"Aśraddadhāna" means those persons lacking faith in this Dharma about to be described,
which is of the nature of knowledge; they, failing to reach Me, return while seized by death.
On the path of saṃsāra. // 3 //
Now he explains that knowledge:
"By me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded;
all beings abide in me, yet I do not abide in them. (BhG 9.4)
"By me": all this has been pervaded by me through my unmanifest form, which is beyond the senses and subtle;
"resting in me" means they abide in me.
And I do not abide in them, because I am established in my own majesty. // 4 //
"Behold my divine yoga"—(and yet, beings do not dwell in Me; behold My divine yoga:
My Self, the sustainer of beings and the source of all beings, does not abide within beings. (BhG 9.5)
1. By means of the form that is beyond the senses;
2. Immediately after the explanation of the fourth verse; 4. //

The syllables "kuṇḍa" are at the edge of those petals; the term "yoga" refers to the commencement of the subsequent petal immediately following. Thus, the syllables "si tvat na ca" are located in the first row, while "iti" is in the second row.
"And not" means: it sustains the elements, thus it is the "sustainer of beings" (bhūtabhṛt); yet it is not within the elements.
Just as the embodied soul (*jīva*) sustains the elements transformed into the form of the body and resides within them, I am not like that.
He is the "creator of beings" because he causes beings to come into existence. // 5 //
Seeing the contradiction in the statement "they abide in me, yet they do not abide in me," He provides an illustration:
"Just as the great wind, moving everywhere, eternally abides in space, so too, understand that all beings abide in me" (BhG 9.6).
Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): just as subtle wind resides in space as something pervasive, omnipresent,
and extending throughout the three worlds, so too understand that the elements abide in Me—
not by way of a relationship of physical contact.
What then? When I, who am all-pervasive, have become the object [of their perception], the [great] elements are of small dimension.
"They revolve" thus indicates the state of duration. // 6 //
Now the state of dissolution is described:
"O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa all beings go to my own nature; again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I emit them forth. (BhG 9.7)
"All," O Kaunteya, means all beings go to my nature at the end of a kalpa; and again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth. // 7 //
How so?—
“Taking hold of my own nature, I project this entire multitude of beings again and again, which is powerless under the sway of nature. (BhG 9.8)
"Prakṛtim" means:
having taken hold of, that is, having relied upon, my own *prakṛti*, I emit the collection of beings (*bhūtagrāma*), the multitude of living entities.
"Helpless" means dependent on the power of *prakṛti*.
Since the *prakṛti* of living beings evolves according to their karma, I create [the world] by virtue of that power.
This refers to "the *prakṛti*s."
What, then, is this primordial nature (*prakṛti*)?
It is the subtle state of the five elements.
It is of the nature of vigor.
In this regard, the method of the Vedānta is as follows: the supreme Brahman, motionless and like space, first existed.
Then, through his wrath, he becomes the internal controller (*antaryāmin*) designated by the term "Lord" (*īśvara*), characterized by the desire to create.
From that, the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), and space (*ākāśa*) arise. From that...
This subtle self is called Hiraṇyagarbha;
from him, the gross great elements, beginning with space, arise in succession.
From that [the Self] came the egg, and from that the Virāj Prajāpati.
Within that gross body of the Virāj—comprising all worlds, all gods, and all beings, both stationary and moving—this [universe] is not the ultimate reality; rather, it is *prakṛti*.
It is mere illusion, lacking any substantial reality. // 8 //
Furthermore, there is no such thing as ignorance (avidyā) other than the notion of a self in that which is not the self;
for the individual soul (jīva), apart from its failure to grasp its own nature as the Supreme Brahman— which exists for each person— nothing else could ever be suspected [as ignorance].
To the objection that there would be fault in one who creates an unequal world, he says:
"And those actions do not bind me, O Dhanañjaya."
"Nor do actions bind Me," he says; why? Because I remain like one who is indifferent (*udāsīna*) toward those actions.
Because of their lack of attachment to those actions, even another person who is attached to the fruit—actions do not bind him either, since the underlying principle is the same. // 9 //
But surely the Sāṅkhyas say that primordial nature (prakṛti) is eternal and independent, and it proceeds toward the creation of the elements; that is incorrect. To this it is said:
"Under my supervision, Nature (prakṛti) produces the world of the moving and the unmoving;

by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the universe revolves. (BhG 9.10) 1. Furthermore, there is no such thing as "ignorance" (avidyā) that exists individually for each person, other than the notion of self (ātma-buddhi) which [the individual soul] holds regarding that which is not the Self. As for the Supreme...
Having set aside the nature of Brahman and its non-apprehension, one might at some point harbor a doubt; therefore, he says: "It may be so," on page 197.
"Mayā" means: having been produced from me with me as the supervisor (adhyakṣa), and being presided over by me as the director (adhiṣṭhātṛ), she brings forth [the world], that is, she generates it.
For the insentient *prakṛti*, consisting of the three *guṇas* as imagined by the Sāṅkhya, cannot function, because it lacks knowledge of the diverse ripening of the karma of living beings.

How is the world, divided into the distinct categories of gods, humans, and animals, created? Furthermore, since it is observed that insentient things such as chariots do not function of their own accord,
it is logical that they operate only when presided over by a conscious agent.
Therefore, nature (prakṛti) is set in motion by me;
by this cause of procreation, the world revolves. // 10 //
"Though I am the presiding lord over nature—
(the foolish disregard me when I have assumed a human form,
not knowing my supreme nature as the great Lord of all beings. BhG 9.11)"
They disregard me; the deluded despise me when I have assumed a human body in my manifestations, thinking, "This is merely a human kṣatriya named Vāsudeva. Thus they treat me with contempt.
Not knowing my supreme state as the Great Lord of all beings. // 11 //
And they—(vain in hope, vain in action, vain in knowledge, and senseless; they have resorted to a delusive nature that is demonic and even fiendish. BhG 9.12.

"Vain" means that their hopes are vain, their actions are vain, and their resolutions are in vain; for their rituals, such as the *agnihotra* and others, are indeed fruitless, and their knowledge is likewise so because its object is not the Self.
Lacking discernment and devoid of discrimination, they abide in a demonic, tamasic nature.
But those great-souled ones, O Pārtha, who abide in the divine nature, worship me with undivided minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings. (BhG 9.13)
1. "By reason of [their] procreation, they are called 'great' (mahā)"; however, those of great soul possess supramundane wisdom and the divine nature (*daivī prakṛti*).
Having known me as the origin of all beings, they resort to and serve me, taking refuge in the mental state born of the quality of goodness (sattva). 13.
In what manner do they worship?— (Constantly chanting my praises and striving with firm vows, bowing down to me with devotion, those who are ever-disciplined worship me. [BhG 9.14]
"Constantly" (*satatatam*) means:

with minds constantly engaged in recounting my true nature, and "striving" (*yatantaḥ*) means making efforts in the means for attaining me; and "firm in their vows" (*dṛḍhavratāḥ*) means having firm, stable [vows].
Those for whom "vow," "restraint," and "action" are not different in meaning are those of firm vows;
and they worship me with devotion and reverence through such activities as prostrating at my feet.
The virtuous, ever-disciplined, worship [Me]. // 14 //

But others, whose knowledge is fully matured— (“And others worship Me with the sacrifice of knowledge; they meditate upon Me as one, as distinct, and in many ways as the one whose face is everywhere,” BhG 9.15).
Regarding the word "jñāna": knowledge itself is the sacrifice, thus it is the "sacrifice of knowledge.
Performing this sacrifice means worshiping, they worship me by practicing meditation upon me.
Worship (*upāsanā*) is the continuous fixing of the mind upon the Supreme Lord.

And they, through the realization that "I am one with Him" and "all this is Vāsudeva," having dissolved the entire manifold of diversity (*prapañca*) into the Supreme Self, the ultimate cause, by means of this [understanding], dissolve their consciousness therein.
They abide in that very Self;
these are the most excellent knowers of Brahman.
Others, however, being unattached in this way, worship [the deities] as distinct entities.
In many ways and by numerous methods,
they meditate upon the Supreme Self in the sun, the moon, and the fire.
Facing all directions, with faces on every side; the origin of all beings.
2. *sthira* 3. *sarvamitya*—these few syllables immediately following this and preceding *samasta* are indistinct.
4. The gates (of that which is) the supreme instrument, p. 199.
That [reality] faces all directions.
Whatever is taken as the objective support, as will be described, that very thing becomes the means for attaining it. // 15 //
He now elaborates upon this:
"I am the sacrifice; I am the offering; I am the ancestral oblation; I am the medicinal herb. I am the mantra; I alone am the clarified butter; I am the fire; I am the oblation. (BhG 9.16)

"I am the sacrifice" (kratu). "I am the sacrifice" refers to the sacrifice characterized by animal and Soma offerings as well as the *iṣṭi* rites, and the Smārta [sacrifices] such as the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*).
That which is performed with reference to the ancestors is *svadhā*. I am the medicinal herb among rice and other grains; what is this? It is food (*anna*).
The mantra consists of the *yājyā*, *puronuvākyā*, and so forth;
I alone am the clarified butter (*ājya*), the means for the oblation; I am the *āhavanīya* fire, into which the offering is poured.
And the oblation is indeed that which is fit for the act of offering. // 16 //
"I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, and the grandfather;
I am the object of knowledge, the purifier, the syllable *oṃ*, and likewise the *Ṛg*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus*.
Regarding the word "father": a father is one who procreates or one who protects.
I alone am the mother, the nurse, the supporter, and the ordainer of the fruits of actions;
I am also the grandfather, the father of one's father.
Whatever object is to be known or understood, that am I; and whatever is pure or purifying, such as expiatory rites and the like, that too am I.
The syllable Om is the Praṇava;
and the three Vedas are indeed myself. 17.
“I am the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the source, the place of dissolution, the treasure-house, and the imperishable seed.
Regarding the word “goal”: it is called a “goal” (*gati*) because it is gone to; I am that which is to be reached.
He is the sustainer, the nourisher;
the lord, the master;
and the witness of actions performed both perceptibly and imperceptibly.
It is the dwelling place of living beings; it is called a "dwelling" because beings dwell within it. It is the refuge for those who are afflicted.
A friend who assists without expectation of recompense;
the source of the world, its dissolution, and its abiding place.
1. That [specific object], 2. such as sacrifice and so forth, 3. such as the *puronuvākyā* (invitatory verse) and so forth.
It is the cause of stability. It is called a "repository" (nidhāna) because in it one's welfare (śreyas) is deposited.
The seed is the cause of origination;
it is imperishable, meaning devoid of decay.
The seeds of rice and other grains, however, are perishable. // 18 //
Moreover:
"I heat; I withhold the rain and I send it forth; I am both immortality and death, and I am being and non-being, O Arjuna. (BhG 9.19)
"I heat," [he says]. Abiding in the form of the sun, I heat with certain rays during the summer season; at the time of the rainy season, I release rain with others.
By my rays I withhold the nectar of life during other seasons;
I am death and destruction, O Arjuna, and I am both the existent and the non-existent.
By "existent" is meant the gross.
An object fit for conventional usage is designated [as existent];
"non-existent" refers to that which is subtle, unmanifest, and beyond conventional usage.
Thus, there is nothing whatsoever apart from me. The wise, who possess right vision, worship me— who am established with faces on all sides— as one, free from desire.
Others, being unwilling [to practice all at once],
worship [the Lord] in many ways through separate individual realizations, such as the sacrifice and so forth.
Such is the summary of the meaning. // 19 //
But those who worship by means of the sacrifice of knowledge— whether as distinct or as one— and those who are mere performers of ritual action, greedy for results—

(Those who know the three Vedas, the drinkers of Soma, purified of sin, having worshipped Me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven; reaching the holy world of the Lord of the Gods, they enjoy divine celestial pleasures in heaven.
1. *kacyantaḥ* (are being praised).
2. This interval contains one indistinct syllable;
immediately following that, the letter *ma* occurs.
After that, there is one indistinct syllable; [as noted] in the *Mūlakośa*, p.
201, it is "traividyā."

Those who possess the three knowledges (*vidyā*) are called *traividyāḥ*; here the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). The meaning is: those who perform the rites prescribed by the three Vedas.
Having drunk the soma and thus purified of sin—with their impurities cleansed by sacrifices—they worship me alone who am established in the form of Indra and others;
yet in reality, they do not know me. They [attain] the heavenly path, the going to heaven. They [attain] merit...
They enjoy the station of Śatakratu, which is attainable through meritorious deeds, and they experience divine pleasures. // 20 //

And they—having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted; thus, following the dharma of the three Vedas and desiring objects of desire, they obtain the state of going and returning. (BhG 9.21)
"Those [beings], having thus enjoyed those pleasures, when their merit is exhausted, upon the depletion of that merit,
enter the world of mortals;
'thus' (evam) refers back to what has been stated."
The word "hi" indicates the reason.
Those who have resorted to the *trayī-dharma*—the ritual action prescribed by the three Vedas—are born and die while desiring objects of pleasure and enjoyments. (21)
"But those people who, thinking of no other, worship Me with constant devotion— to them, who are ever-exerting themselves, I provide both acquisition and preservation. (BhG 9.22)
"Thinking of Me as having no other":
those for whom there is no other object of worship are "ananya"; for them, who are constantly engaged [in yoga], I alone provide *yogakṣema*.
Yoga is the attainment of what has not yet been attained;
security is the preservation of what has been attained.
Both of these constitute [yoga]. // 22 //
1. Departure;

2. "When enjoyments have been consumed" means when your pleasures have been exhausted; for those whose merit is spent, upon the exhaustion of the merit of Śatakratu, that which was achieved through karma [is lost].
It appears that the reading from "atra rma" up to this point is corrupt.
3. Traidharnya.
Furthermore:
"Even those who, devoted to other deities, worship them endowed with faith..."
"Even they, O son of Kuntī, sacrifice to me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding the phrase "even those who": even those who are devotees of other deities and sacrifice—meaning they worship—with faith, they indeed sacrifice to me.
They too, in reality, worship me alone; however, it is not according to the prescribed rule. The meaning is that it is devoid of the method for the path to liberation.
Furthermore, they do not know the procedure prescribed by the Kalpasūtras, which is preceded by the [proper] ritual injunctions. // 23 //
But why is it so?—(For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the lord of all sacrifices; yet they do not recognize me in truth, and therefore they fall. [BhG 9.24]
"I indeed" means: for I am the enjoyer and the sovereign lord of all sacrifices, abiding in the various forms of Indra and the other gods;
yet they do not recognize me.
[They are] thus established in reality;
therefore, they fall from that state.
The meaning is that they undergo a return [to this world]. // 24 //
He demonstrates this very point:
"Those devoted to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and those who worship me go to me. (BhG 9.25)
"They go" means they go as those devoted to the gods (*devavratāḥ*),
whose vow is the work of the gods. As is one's resolve (*kratu*) in this world, so does one become after passing away from here.

Thus says the Śruti; and there is also the Brāhmaṇa passage: "In whatever way one worships him... This is explained by the word itself (nigada-vyākhyā). Therefore, all [who worship] me are sacrificers (yājinaḥ).
They become Vāsudevas. // 25 //
1. They do not know the ritual procedure taught in the Kalpasūtras; 2. by means of this or that [form], he abides in the nature of Indra and others; 3. thus he abides.
...its fruitfulness is through this... recite... because it is that which is to be accomplished... he is to be propitiated.
How so?
"Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—that offering made with devotion by one of purified soul, I accept. (BhG 9.26).
"A leaf, a flower," and so forth.
The leaves are those of the *vilva* and other such trees; the flowers are those of the *karavīra* and others;
the fruits are those of the *badara*, the mango, and so forth.
Thinking, "My birth has achieved its purpose," with a heart moistened by affection, I accept what he offers and eat it; thus, through the intellect of faith, I am satisfied. (26)
Since this is so, therefore:
"Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī—perform that as an offering unto Me. (BhG 9.27)
Regarding the word "yat" (whatever): whatever one does, such as bathing and so forth;
whatever one eats at the time of eating—the *prāṇāhuti* (oblation to the vital breaths) is thereby indicated.
Whatever you offer in the external fire, whatever gold and other gifts you give, and whatever austerity you perform, such as fasting— make all that an offering unto Me. (27)
Hear then the fruit thereof:
"In this way, by the fruits of both good and evil, you shall be released from the bonds of karma;
with your self disciplined by the yoga of renunciation, liberated, you shall come unto Me. (BhG 9.28)
Regarding "auspicious": those bonds of karma which have auspicious and inauspicious fruits—
karma itself being the bonds—
you are liberated from them.
And he is liberated, his self being disciplined through the yoga of renunciation (*sannyāsa*). Renunciation is the dedication of performed actions to Brahman; that indeed is it.
The yoga is the cultivation of non-difference regarding the agent, the object, and the fruit;
the self is joined with these two.
He whose self is disciplined by this yoga of renunciation shall come to Me.

Now, one might object: "If indeed only he who performs the act of surrender to you approaches you while still possessing passion and other such defects, then you would be like a king in the world who benefits only his devotee and not another.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"I am impartial toward all beings; to Me there is none hateful and none dear.
But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I also am in them. (BhG 9.29).
Regarding the phrase "I am impartial":

I am impartial toward all beings; I have neither attachment nor aversion. It is my very nature to bestow grace upon whoever worships me with devotion, just as fire removes cold and other discomforts for one who approaches it properly, but not for anyone else. Therefore, those who...
But those who worship, serve, and take refuge in me with devotion— I abide within them; here,
passion and hatred are not the cause, but rather [devotion].
The intention is: "I favor [beings] like fire by demonstrating results that correspond to the karma of living beings. // 29 //
Now, even by way of refuting [the necessity of] conduct and so forth, an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is made for the purpose of praising the taking of refuge in the Blessed One.
He says that conduct (*vṛtta*) is also a factor here:
"Even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, he is to be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved.
(BhG 9.30) Regarding the word "even" (*api*): even if he is one of exceedingly (*suṣṭhu*) and intensely (*bhṛśam*) wicked conduct, he is indeed righteous.
He should be consulted; why?
Because he has rightly resolved, possesses a well-ascertained intellect, and stands firmly upon the true path.
The word "hi" indicates the reason. // 30 //
Furthermore, this view— [p. 205] —is as follows:
"Quickly he becomes righteous in nature and attains eternal peace;
O Kaunteya, declare this with certainty: my devotee perishes not.
Regarding the word "quickly":
... ṭi ... from the destruction of evil.
"Perpetually" (*śaśvat*) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*);
the meaning is that it "goes forth."
Therefore, recognize this truth:
my devotee does not perish. // 31 //

Now, regarding the service of the Lord that was introduced with the words "But those who worship Me with devotion," this [verse] is intended to explain the taking of refuge in the Lord through faith and devotion.
He also states an explanatory passage (arthavāda):
"For even those who may be of low birth— women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras— even they, O Pārtha, attain the supreme goal by taking refuge in Me" (BhG 9.32).
Regarding the word "mām" (me): O Pārtha, those who, having taken refuge in me—having specifically relied upon me as their shelter—even though they are of sinful birth;
that is, those whose birth or origin is from sin, are called "pāpayonayaḥ."
Even those of low birth, such as women and others who are entirely ineligible for liberation,
shall attain the supreme [state] through the destruction of their sins by fulfilling my command, which is characterized by the performance of their own duties.
It is considered certain that they go to— that is, they attain— the preeminent and supreme state characterized by heaven;
for contact with me is a cause of purification, just as contact with fire is for iron.
"Serve me with your own duty," because it is prescribed that propitiation is to be performed by one's own duty alone,
even for a Śūdra, the act of rising to greet is born of his own nature; thus, [he should serve] by rising to greet.
"A human being attains that very fulfillment of purpose through his own duty consisting of service.
This is because the accomplishment of the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha) will be established precisely through the performance of that [duty]. // 32 //
1. Concluding the purport of the explanatory passage (arthavāda) with the words "by one's own action" (*svakarmaṇāsevyā*) on page 206, he says: [1]—
"What then [to speak of] the meritorious Brahmins, or likewise the devoted royal sages?
Having reached this world which is impermanent and full of suffering, worship Me!
(BhG 9.33). Why [is this said]? For even women and others who are not [ordinarily] qualified, once they have taken refuge in the Blessed One, become superior.
They go to their respective destinies; how much more so those of pure birth who are authorized— namely, the brahmins and royal seers?

And [the phrase] "they will not go" is used with the word *api* in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*) as a hyperbolic expression (*atiśayokti*) to inspire interest in knowledge among the Brahmins and others; it does not mean the literal sense as it is heard.

It is prescribed as follows: "One might even split a mountain with one's head; one might even eat a meal cooked by Droṇa"—by this sentence, the confidence in human capability is established, but not the splitting of the mountain itself.
It is not being established because of its impossibility;
for since the statement "one should split a mountain" has another purpose and lacks intentionality toward its own literal meaning, there is no engagement with it. Indeed, not...
The cessation [of an action] occurs through the praise of a matter enjoined by injunction and through the censure of a prohibited and evil matter, such as the cooking of *droṇa* rice;
however, one's own purpose characterized by the consumption of poison is not thereby established. And for this reason:
Jaimini composed the sūtra defining the nature of *arthavāda*: "But because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, they exist for the purpose of praising the injunctions.
These are the *arthavādas*.

The meaning is that, by virtue of being syntactically connected with an injunction— either as a supplement to an injunction or as a supplement to a prohibition— they would serve either to praise that [injunction] or to censure it;
for the sentences of the *arthavāda* constitute the meaning of words and lack any intentionality (*tātparya*) toward their own literal sense.
"And because it is intent upon something else.

Thus it has been said by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda himself: "That which is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning a quality from that which is to be explained, being not [itself] intent upon that..."
"If one desires to comprehend the meaning, how could its truth be established?

Thus it is said in the Śruti: "In the animal sacrifice, the offering of the omentum (vapā) must be performed. For the mandatory execution of this injunction, there is an explanatory passage (arthavāda):

Prajāpati cut out the omentum (1). He speaks of the withdrawal (2). For [the prohibition] "one should not [eat] the joint... is not for the sake of another, but has its purport toward its own meaning; for indeed... by way of praise, there is the cessation of that which was prohibited... the application of the rule... and Jaimiti says...
2. Regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*) on page 207, etc., its meaning is as follows: in this manner, the sacrificer must necessarily perform the offering of the omentum (*vapāhoma*).
"It must be performed.

This refers to what was stated [regarding] the injunction for the animal sacrifice: that in the absence of another animal, Prajāpati himself performed the offering of the omentum after having torn out his own omentum.
The excision of one's own entrails is superimposed [as a duty] for the sake of incitement, even though it is not actually required;
this is just as in the world, where one avoids eating at the house of a wicked person who is undesired, for the sake of deterrence.
Someone says: "It is better to eat poison than to eat in his house.
Even by this worldly explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), the act of eating poison itself is not enjoined as its own primary meaning; rather, it is [intended] through hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
...the abstention from eating at home is practiced;
... it is prohibited ...
1. messenger.
2. characterized by the consumption of garlic.
